Introduction. A Brief History Of Radiology

Sorin M. Dudea

The discovery, on November 8, 1895, by Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen, of X-rays, represents the birth certifificate of a, then, new medical discipline – radiology – as well as the beginning of the fascinating path that led, today, to the possibility of achieving actual “dissections” by images of the patient.

In 1896, Thomas Edison produced the fifirst functional radioscopy device. The fifirst radiology technicians appeared in 1903. In 1913 the Coolidge tube was invented for the controlled production of X-rays. George Eastman invented the radiological fifilm in 1918.

Bismuth, lead and barium salts have been used experimentally as contrast agents since 1896. In the early 1920s, iodine’s accidental discovery as a contrast agent changed radiology: the fifirst pyelogram was obtained in 1923 and the fifirst in vivo angiography in 1924. In 1929 Werner Forssmann performed – on himself – the fifirst venous catheterization of the heart and thus opened the way for cardiac catheterization, diagnostic and interventional radiological procedures.

As a screening method, mammography was developed in the late 1950s; ultrasonography was fifirst used for medical diagnostic purposes in the mid-1950s. Plane tomography, as a method of obtaining the image of a section through the human body using X-rays, was performed in the early 1900s. The fifirst computed tomography image ( CT) was obtained in 1971. The fifirst magnetic resonance image (MRI) was obtained in 1977.

One cannot omit the remarkable role of the discovery, in 1896, of natural radioactivity by Antoine Becquerel. Irene and Frederic Joliot – Curie discovered, in the early 1930s, the artifificial radionuclides. These discoveries led to the emergence of nuclear medicine. The methods that use gamma radiation emitted by isotopes represent a medical specialty’s prerogative – nuclear medicine – different from radiology in most European countries.

The recognition of the importance of X-ray and radioactivity discoveries is certifified by the Nobel Prizes awarded concerning these fifields. Some of these awards are Wilhelm Roentgen in 1901 (X-rays), Pierre and Marie Curie and Henri Becquerel in 1903 (radioactivity), Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie (1935), Allan Cormack and Godfrey Hounsfifield in 1979 (computer tomography), Paul Lautebur and Peter Mansfifield in 2003 (nuclear magnetic resonance).

Today, the exponential development of radiological techniques’ applications makes the multimodal explorations charac4 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS teristic of the four major classes of imaging methods – conventional radiology, ultrasonography, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging – intertwine with each other but also with applications of nuclear medicine (SPECT, PET), performing fusion imaging. Increasingly, today’s imaging means not only anatomy and function but also metabolic and molecular diagnosis.

Elemental Physics And Technique In Conventional Radiology

Călin Schiau

2.1 Physical principle

Conventional radiography is a technique based on the analysis of a beam of X-rays’ attenuation as it passes through tissue.

The Roentgen radiation (or X-ray) is high-frequency electromagnetic radiation. It is a form of ionizing radiation, as it produces ionization in matter that it crosses; it is composed of photons.

The X-ray occurs in the form of a photonic energy flflow on the surface of the radiogenic tube’s anode (radiation source). From here emerges the radiation beam (the vector) directed towards the examined body (modulator) inside of which the beam undergoes changes that depend on the structure of the examined body. The modulated beam arrives to the receiver (primary analog image), which processes it digitally, resulting in a secondary digital picture (processed) with a higher diagnostic value. From here, the image reaches the fifinal station where the decoder (equipment user, physician) will analyze and integrate the obtained information in a clinical and biological context and with the information of previous radio-imaging examinations.

2.2. Structure of matter

The atom represents the smallest constituent unit of matter that retains all the chemical element’s characteristics, being chemically further indivisible.

Every atom is composed of a nucleus and one or more electrons. Every nucleus is composed of one or more protons and neutrons.

The mass of the atom concentrates in the nucleus. An atom is characterized by two numbers: A and Z. Z = atomic number = the total number of

protons within the nucleus / electrical

charges; A = mass number = the total number of

nucleons (protons or neutrons). The relation between the two numbers is

A ≥ Z.

The electrons orbit the nucleus in one of the ‘shells’ surrounding the nucleus, labeled K, L, M, N, from the center outwards. As long as they are located on a predefifined orbit, the electrons’ movement occurs without gaining or losing energy.

The electrons in an atom move from a lower energy level (inner orbit) to a higher energy level (outer orbit) by gaining the required energy. An electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level by losing energy. The energy shift is 6 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS expressed in quantas and is given by the formula:

E = hν (h = Plank constant, ν = frequency of the

emitted or absorbed radiation).

2.3 Basic physics

2.3.1 Wave – represents the propagation of a disturbance producing in its path a reversible variation of local physical properties. It transports energy without transporting matter.

A wave is periodic if the associated disturbance is repeated identically over time. Period, frequency, and wavelength are the characteristics of any periodic wave.

2.3.2. Period is the time necessary for a periodic phenomenon to repeat itself. It is labeled T. The measurement unit for the period is the second (s).

2.3.3. The frequency of the wave, labeled ν, and expressed in Hertz (Hz), is related to the period by the relation:

ν = 1 / T

2.3.4. Wavelength is the spatial equivalent of the period. It corresponds to the distance traveled by the wave over a period. It is also called the space period. It is labeled λ and is expressed in metric units (m).

The formula that links wavelength (λ), period (T), speed of propagation (c), and frequency (ν) of the wave is: λ = cT = c / ν.

2.3.5. The photon is an elementary particle that makes up electromagnetic radiation and is a mediator of its action. It is characterized by an energy proportional to the frequency of the considered electromagnetic wave (E = hν) and inversely proportional to wavelength (E = hc/λ).

2.3.6. The electromagnetic rad i­

ation is a disturbance of the magnetic fifield and the electric fifield. It is produced by perpendicular electric and magnetic fifields, oscillating in phase. Its vector is the photon. The electromagnetic waves are a representation of this phenomenon. They are a set of similar nature waves (not requiring a material medium to propagate) but characterized by different wavelengths. They include radio waves, microwaves, infrared rays, visible rays, ultraviolet (UV), X-rays, and gamma rays (fifigure 1).

2.3.7. Ionizing radiation

Ionization designates ions’ production, which occurs as a consequence of adding or removing electrical charges from an atom or molecule. Ionizing radiation is the term given to forms of radiation that are energetic enough to displace orbiting electrons from the absorbing medium’s atoms, thus forming positive ions. Ions can dissipate their energy in matter and, as a consequence, may cause biomolecular damage. The ionization energy is measured in electron volts.

2.4. Steps in obtaining an X­ray image

The steps for obtaining a radiographic image are X-ray production, absorption, and detection. The latter will be detailed along with the radiologic equipment.

2.4.2 Propagation through the object

The X-ray beam is directed towards the object to explore. As it crosses the object, the beam undergoes variable absorption (or attenuation), which depends on three factors:

2. ELEMENTAL PHYSICS AND TEC

  • the thickness of the materials crossed; the thicker the material, the greater the absorption of the X-ray beam;
  • the nature of the tissues; each material is characterized by its own absorption coeffificient;
  • radiation energy: the higher the X-ray energy, the lower the X-ray absorption in tissues.

IMPORTANT!

The absorption (or attenuation) coeffificient

The fundamental notion in conventional radiography is that of density. Radiographic density is a physical quantity which depends on the coeffificient of absorption (or attenuation) of X-rays by each tissue.

This absorption coeffificient varies depending on the chemical composition of the matter. It is high for materials composed of high atomic number atoms, such as bone, containing calcium. It is weaker for soft tissue composed mainly of oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, or nitrogen, with low atomic number atoms.

High absorption coeffificient tissues strongly attenuate X-rays. Otherwise, if the absorption coeffificient is low, the attenuation is poor.

2.5. Characteristics and properties of X­rays

The X-ray beam is characterized by frequency and wavelength, the latter located between gamma and ultraviolet radiation. The wavelength of the beam determines the penetration.

Filtration is an operation of homogenization and hardening of the beam by CHNIQUE IN CONVENTIONAL RADIOLOGY l 9 removing low-energy radiation from the beam. This low energy radiation is useless for diagnosis because it is absorbed, interacting strongly with living matter.

Soft X­rays: have higher wavelength (λ = 1-5 nm), and lower energy and penetrability;

Hard X­rays: have a shorter wavelength (λ = 0.01 nm) and higher energy and penetrability.

X­ray properties:

  • They spread spherically from the point of origin;
  • They are invisible and propagate in a straight line with the speed of light;
  • In the air, their intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the source;
  • Penetrate bodies that are opaque for light; their penetrability is inversely propor- tional to the wavelength;
  • Are absorbed and emitted in characteristic amounts for each chemical element (wave-corpus duality  photon);
  • Are absorbed by the bodies they cross – Bragg – Pierce relation. The relation that defifines x-ray absorption at the level of a material body is: A=Z4 λ 3 ρdΔt, where:
  • A is the absorption;
  • Z is the atomic number of the body crossed by X-radiation;
  • λ is the radiation wavelength (depending on the voltage applied to the X-ray tube);
  • ρ is the density of the crossed body;
  • d is the thickness of the crossed body;
  • Δt is the exposure time to the X-rays.
  • Produce the photoelectric effect or lu- minescence (phosphorescence, flfluores- cence).
  • Produce the photosensitive effect (photo- chemical) through the photolytic effect.< 10 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS

  • Produce ionization
  • Produce biological effects.
  • Are not deviated by electric or magnetic fifields (they have no charge; they have no mass).
  • May undergo optical phenomena such as refraction, diffraction and polarization.

2.7.2. Fluoroscopy

It represents a real-time X-ray exam with high temporal resolution. In addition to morphological information, it can provide functional information.

The direct receptor is a screen (scintillation plate).

The operating principle  flfluorescence: light emission occurs as long as the atom is subjected to incident radiation. Basic appearance:

  • transparency = white (x-rays reach the screen  light emission – photoelectric effect);
  • opacity = black (x-rays do not reach the screen).

The technique is based on an X-ray image intensififier that converts X-rays emerging from the patient into an optical image. The intensififier is coupled to a still/ video camera, and the image is projected on a monitor.

The primary use of this method, nowadays, is interventional radiology. Occasionally, flfluoroscopy is used for the radio12 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS logical examination of the gastrointestinal and urinary tract; however, it implies highdose radiation exposures!

2.7.3. Analogic radiography

The operating principle  phosphorescence: the emission of light also occurs after the cessation of X-ray action.

Basic appearance:

  • transparency = black (the incident rays are not absorbed and reach the fifilm in the cassette, respectively, the photographic emulsion, resulting in the dissociation of the silver bromide molecule; the metallic silver blackens the fifilm);
  • opacity = white (the incident rays are absorbed; they do not reach the fifilm, which, after processing, remains transparent – white).

The receiver has several components: an anti-diffuser grid (removes secondary radiation) and the radiographic fifilm’s cassette with intensifying screens.

Radiography is a less irradiating method compared to flfluoroscopy. It offers exclusively morphological information.

The main clinical applications are in emergency medicine: trauma (e.g., fractures), acute thoracic (pneumothorax, acute pulmonary edema), or abdominal (urolithiasis, intestinal obstruction) disorders.

2.7.4. Digital radiography

The technique is based on discrete values compared to conventional radiography, which uses analog/continuous values. It removes the requirement of darkroom procedures.

There are two types of digital radiography: ­ computed radiography (CR): uses pho-

tostimulable phosphorus plates (PSP):

materials that store absorbed energy

within excited electrons and release it

in the form of light on exposure to

laser energy. They replace the analog

fifilm in the cassettes. The plate can be

‘reset’ and reused repeatedly.

  • direct digital radiography (DDR): direct digital registration of the detector’s image with no need for a cassette.

2.7.5. Dedicated types of Roentgen devices

The mammograph offers the possibility of a breast X-ray in two standard views.

The angiograph provides vascular exploration by using a contrast agent and X-rays.

The dental X-ray machines are used for orthopantomography (panoramic dental X-ray), intraoral digital radiography, AP teleradiography and CBCT computed tomography.

The Radiographic Image

Ioana Bene, Anca Ciure

The radiographic image is the twodimensional image formed by the passage of X-rays through a volume (the patient’s anatomic area of interest). During exposure, X-rays emitted by the tube form a cone-shaped primary X-ray beam.

3.1. Scatter radiation

When the primary X-ray beam interacts with the patient, a part of its energy is absorbed, resulting in scatter radiation,

To prevent scattered radiation from reaching the IR, one uses the Bucky grid, a device placed between the tabletop and the IR. 3.2 Image formation

The tissues absorb radiation differently, depending on their density. Uneven absorption results in a pattern with different intensities in the X-ray beam exiting the patient’s opposite side. The intensity of the opacity on an image may be produced by the summation effect (by overlapping two or more opaque structures located in the same direction but different planes) or by the subtraction effect (by overlapping of tructures located in the same direction but different an opaque with a lucent structure located in the same fect an opaque with a lucent structure) (fifigure 7).

The IR can be represented by a flfluorescent screen (produces a flfluoroscopic image), a traditional cassette containing a fifilm, or a digital radiation receiver (obtaining a radiographic image). These days, digital images are widely used, and most flfluoroscopic units can produce both radiography and flfluoroscopy.

3.3. Factors influencing the radiographic exposure

3.3.1. Exposure time represents the amount of time that X-rays are emitted, measured in seconds, fractions of seconds, or milliseconds. A long exposure time results in an increased production of X-rays and a darker radiographic image, while a decrease in exposure time produces a lighter image.

3.3.2. Milliamperage (mA) mea-

sures the electric power flflow rate in the X-ray tube circuit, indicating the number of electrons available for bombarding the anode. Milliamperage determines the brightness of the image. Therefore, a high milliamperage increases the X-rays’ intensity and implicitly increases the image’s brightness on flfluoroscopy (or image darkness on radiography) and vice versa (fifigure 8).

3.3.3. The kilovoltage determines the energy and the penetrability of the X-ray beam. On radiography, high kilovoltage produces a darker image and decreases the image contrast, while low kilovoltage produces a brighter image and increases the

3.6. Pearls and Pitfalls

All radiographs must include annotations (date, patient’s name and identifification number, right or left marker, institution identity).

The radiographer must prevent the appearance of confusing densities on the radiograph by straightening any folds in the clothes and by removing radiopaque objects (earrings, snaps, necklaces, buttons, zippers).

Contrast Media In Radiology

Anca Ciurea, Ioana Ben

Contrast media (CM) in radiology are defifined as agents used to improve the contrast resolution of an imaging method to better visualize and characterize the pathological lesions.

CM is used with all imaging methods (X-ray, CT, ultrasound and MRI). In conventional radiology and CT, they alter how different structures absorb X-rays. On ultrasound and MRI, they change the response of tissues to the ultrasound beam or magnetic fifield. In this way, they create a contrast between different normal structures or normal and abnormal tissues with otherwise similar appearance, diffificult to differentiate on native (non-contrast) examinations.

In radiology, CM is used to visualize tubular structures (e.g., blood vessels, the gastrointestinal tract), visualize lesions not otherwise seen, increase the conspicuity and better characterize the lesions.

Depending on the type of image (contrast) they produce (“black or white”), CM are classifified into negative and positive contrast agents.

In radiology, the negative contrast media agents attenuate the X-rays less than the body’s soft tissues and induce a lucent/ hypodense image. Oppositely, the positive contrast agents attenuate X-rays more than ne the body’s soft tissues and produce an opaque/hyperdense image.

The negative contrast agents used are air (in flfluoroscopy examinations such as double-contrast enema) (fifigure 12), carbon dioxide (insuflflated into the colon in CT colonography), and superparamagnetic agents (used in MRI, for certain pathological conditions).

Fig. 12. Double-contrast barium enema, performed with barium and air. Note the negative contrast produced by the air.

All the other agents used in conventional radiology, CT, MRI, and ultrasound produce a positive contrast.

4.1. Contrast media used in X­ray examinations

4.1.1. Barium sulfate is a suspension of insoluble particles of barium. It is administered orally or per rectum to visualize the gastrointestinal tubular structures (esophagrams, upper gastrointestinal series, small bowel follow-throughs, rectography, and barium enema) (fifigure 13). Their use is generally restricted to radiographic and flfluoroscopic examinations, but, occasionally, very low-density dilution may also be used for CT examination of the GI tract.

Fig. 13. Barium swallow and small bowel follow-through in a patient with esophagoplasty for an esophagus carcinoma.

4. CONTRAST MEDIA IN RADIOLOGY l 19

Contraindications

Due to its insolubility in the gut, very little toxic barium passes through the gastrointestinal tract wall and is absorbed in the body. Even if well-tolerated by most patients, with infrequent complications occurring due to its use, administration or leakage of barium outside the intestinal tract may have severe adverse effects.

The contraindications for the administration of barium sulfate are:

  • suspicion of gastrointestinal perforation
  • in the peritoneal cavity, the barium causes inflflammation and peritonitis;
  • colonic obstruction – if there is a delay in the evacuation of the barium suspen- sion, it may become inspissated and aggravate the obstruction;
  • considerable volume aspiration risk – even if a small amount is less irritating for the lung parenchyma compared with hyperosmolar contrast media, barium is contraindicated in large esophage- al-bronchial fifistulas or esophagus per- foration;
  • known allergy to barium (very rare).

4.1.2. Iodinated contrast media are

based on a benzene ring to which three iodine atoms are attached. A monomer contains one tri-iodinated benzene ring, and a dimer has two tri-iodinated benzene rings.

Classification

Iodinated contrast media can be ionic or non-ionic. Ionic iodinated contrast media are no longer used due to the increased risk of anaphylactic reactions.

Another classifification of the iodinated contrast media relates to their osmolality (compared to the osmolality of plasma), which classififies them in high-, low- and iso-osmolar agents. The osmolality also inflfluences the risk of adverse reactions, the incidence being higher for high osmolar 20 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS agents. The ideal iodinated contrast media should be non-ionic and iso-osmolar to minimize the risk of side effects.

Iodinated contrast media are water-soluble, with only one water-insoluble product available in the present. The only indications for the use of water-insoluble agents are hysterosalpingography, sialography and embolo-/sclerotherapy.

Administration

Iodinated contrast media can be administered orally, intravenously, intra-arterial or intra-cavitary. They are used in many types of examinations to visualize different structures:

  • esophagus, stomach and gut (when there is a contraindication for barium ad- ministration or in CT examination, to produce contrast between the intesti- nal loops and other structures) (fifigure 14);
  • blood vessels (conventional or digital angiography, phlebography, angioCT);
  • bile ducts (cholangiography);
  • urinary tract (intravenous pyelography, re- trograde or percutaneous pyelography, urethrography, cystography and CT urography);
  • joint space (arthrography);
  • spine (myelography and myeloCT – repla- ced by MRI and used only for patients with contraindications for MRI exami- nation);
  • parenchymal organs (on CT).

Kinetics (timing phase of contrast media for CT)

After the intravenous (iv) administration of iodinated contrast media, due to X-rays attenuation by iodine, the contrast will produce the opacifification of different structures in the body. Transient dysfunction becomes more severe if the renal function is impaired before contrast administration. Radiobiology

Andrei Roman

The diagnostic (radiography, flfluoroscopy and CT) and interventional (flfluoroscopy) imaging techniques that employ X-rays to depict the human body’s internal structures are widely used in modern medical practice. As these techniques, mainly CT, have become more widespread, medical radiation exposure has risen signifificantly in the general population, increasing the risk for radiation-induced health effects. To prevent and manage these risks, understanding the effects of ionizing radiation on living organisms is necessary. There are three phases of interaction of the ionizing radiation with the living matter: physical, chemical and biological.

9.1. Physical and chemical effects of radiation on the living cell

a. Physical effects

In a living organism targeted by an X-ray beam, some photons pass through without interacting with molecules, while the rest are absorbed by the molecules they meet. After the absorption of a photon, an electron is ejected from its orbit. The molecule becomes ionized, either through the Compton or the photoelectric effect. The ejected electron will hit and ionize nearby molecules until it depletes its energy, thus creating a cluster of ionizations.

b. Chemical effects

Ionized molecules are more likely to break their preexisting chemical bonds and react with other molecules, thus altering their original function. This process can affect any cell molecules; most of them, such as membrane components, proteins, RNA, can easily be replaced without vital importance. However, DNA is especially vulnerable to radiation damage due to its considerable molecular size and the fact that there are only two copies of it in each cell. DNA also holds the vast majority of information necessary for the normal functioning of the cell. Its integrity is vital for the highly complex and sensitive mitotic process.

DNA can be damaged through direct interaction with radiation or indirectly through interaction with other ionized molecules, most frequently hydroxyl radicals (OH-). As approximately 60% of a human’s weight is represented by water, there is a high likelihood that the X-rays will interact with, and ionize water molecules, thus creating highly reactive free hydroxyl radicals. These radicals have a long enough lifespan to diffuse in the DNA’s proximity and react with it, producing an estimated two-thirds of all X-ray related damage.

Radiation-induced DNA alteration can take the form of individual and multiple base damage, intra- or inter-molecular crosslinking and single- or double-strand breaks, the latter usually being most harmful to the cell.

All the physical and chemical processes described so far occur within less than one millisecond after radiation exposure. From here on, the biological effects begin and they may span over weeks, months or even decades.

9.2. Radiation­induced cell death (deterministic effects)

After the DNA has been affected by radiation, one or more cellular damage response pathways are activated.

A highly effective DNA repair system can correct most alterations while the cell’s progression through the cell cycle is temporarily blocked.

In some situations, when extensive damage has occurred and is detected by the cellular regulating mechanisms, the cell cycle can be blocked permanently or apoptosis steps in. Besides apoptosis, cell death can also occur through the processes of necrosis, autophagy and senescence or the so-called mitotic catastrophe.

The mitotic catastrophe is the main mechanism by which tissues are affected by radiation. Cellular division is an exact mechanism; therefore, unrepaired DNA damage leads to defective mitosis. A series of defective divisions induces an accumulation of errors until, after a few generations, the cells cannot replicate and die. This situation poses a particular problem for tissues with high division rates, such as the basal layer of the epidermis, erythroblasts and spermatogenetic precursors. There is a constant need to

9. RADIOBIOLOGY l 81 replace cells dying through natural causes in these tissues, which is satisfified by the precursor cells’ sustained rapid divisions. If there is a signifificant imbalance between cell death and the tissue’s ability to replace them, tissue function loss occurs and acute radiation symptoms become noticeable.

The time interval between exposure and symptoms onset, as well as the duration and severity of the symptoms depend, among others, on the natural lifespan of the cells and the radiation dose.

Acute radiation effects caused by radiation-induced cell death usually appear within 90 days after exposure and, in most cases, remit allowing complete recovery. If the radiation dose is high enough in specifific tissues, complete depletion of a particular cell line can occur. This circumstance leads to a total loss of organ function; for example, radiation damage to the testes can lead to sterility. Cells with low mitotic rates (liver, kidney, pancreas) or those that have lost the ability to divide and have long lifespans (neurons) are the most resistant to radiation. This observation can be explained by the fact that DNA damage is usually less relevant for the cell’s routine activities than for the susceptible division process, allowing the cells to survive despite the genetic material’s damage. These cells have more time between divisions for the DNA repair mechanisms to step in and are less susceptible to apoptosis.

Late radiation effects occur independently from the early reactions and have intricate mechanisms such as abnormal proliferation of fifibroblasts leading to increased collagen deposition and tissue fifibrosis. Such effects have a slow evolution over the years and are irreversible.

The previously described acute and chronic radiation effects are determin- istic, meaning that they are known to reliably appear after a certain organ-specifific

The threshold is explained by the fact that the repair and recovery mechanisms can compensate for a certain amount of damage (number of lost cells) until tissue dysfunction becomes manifest. The cerebrovascular syndrome appears at a total dose of approximately 100 Gy and results in death in 24 to 48 h through intracranial hypertension due to capillary damage and leakage. Central nervous system related clinical manifestations may span from fatigue, headache, dizzyness to stupor, seizures, loss of consciousness and coma.

9.3. Cancer induction (stochastic effect)

Deterministic effects appear through tissue damage after radiation-induced cell death. If, after exposure, the DNA of a cell has sustained unrepaired damage, but the cell has survived and has maintained its ability to replicate, the DNA alteration is transmitted to its daughter cells. Most of these mutations do not have any signifificant consequences. However, some will lead to cancer if somatic cells are affected or to heritable effects if the gametes are affected.

These effects are called stochastic (random) because their occurrence is not bound by a dose threshold, but by chance. Theoretically, even a single photon can trigger a mutation that will eventually lead to cancer. However, a higher dose will lead to an increased chance of these mutations

9.4. Prenatal radiation exposure (stochastic and deterministic effects)

The effects of radiation on a developing embryo or fetus can be stochastic or deterministic. Prenatal exposure to radiation, especially in the last trimester, can signifificantly increase childhood cancer risks through the same mechanisms as in adults, especially leukemia (stochastic effect). There is also evidence that in utero exposure is associated with a higher risk of solid tumors later in life.

Non-cancer effects of radiation are deterministic, meaning that there are no manifestations below a threshold (0,05 Gy) at any stage of gestation and are mainly caused by radiation-induced cell death. These effects depend on the radiation dose and the developmental stage at which the exposure occurs.

Thus, in the fifirst two weeks after conception, there is an “all or nothing” effect where the embryo either dies and is aborted or develops without signifificant abnormalities.

There is an increased risk of major malformations in the organogenesis stage (2-7 weeks).

In the early fetogenesis period (8-15 weeks), there is a small risk of signifificant malformations at high doses, but the main effects will be microcephaly and mental retardation.

During the later phases of fetogenesis, only higher doses (>0,5 Gy) will be harmful, leading to growth restriction and, less frequently, to mental retardation.

At higher doses, miscarriage is possible during all stages of pregnancy.

9.5. Radiation exposure of gonads (stochastic and deterministic effects)

Radiation exposure of the gonads can induce sterility in both men and women, which is a deterministic effect caused by cell death.

In men, exposure at lower doses can induce temporary sterility that will recover in a few months to years as the surviving spermatogonia replace the cells killed by radiation.

However, women have a limited number of oocytes that have ceased dividing soon after birth and cannot be replaced. For this reason, any damage is defifinitive and there is no temporary sterility in women. However, there is a marked difference in radiosensitivity, prepubertal females being six times more resistant than premenopausal women.

If a germ cell suffers non-lethal alterations of its genetic material, not repaired before fertilization, these alterations may be transmitted to the offspring causing a mutation. This is a stochastic effect as there is no dose limit involved, even the slightest exposure being able to cause alterations. The mutations that occur are not specifific to radiation exposure; there is only a dose-proportional increase of the mutations that spontaneously appear under natural circumstances.

Therefore, exposure of the gonads to radiation has a theoretical potential to increase the risk of known mendelian, chromosomal or multifactorial diseases. These effects have been studied and are well-known from animal models. However, in practice, the risk is very low as no signifificant increase in the incidence of such diseases has been noticed after a life-long observation of the Japanese atom bomb survivors’ offspring.

Dosimetry And Radioprotection

Andrei Roman

Radiation protection has the purpose of protecting people from the harmful effects of exposure to ionizing radiation. To estimate the risk of developing radiation-induced health effects (deterministic or stochastic), one must know the radiation dose to which someone has been exposed. This is no simple task, as sometimes a direct measurement is not possible. Different types of radiation have different effects on living tissue and different tissues have different sensitivities to the same dose of radiation. Therefore, multiple measurement units for radiation exposure are being used, among which the most common are the absorbed dose, equivalent dose and effective dose.

10.1. Dosimetry

The absorbed dose is defifined as the energy absorbed per unit of mass and is measured in gray (1 Gy = 1 J/kg). In diagnostic and interventional radiology, the absorbed dose can be directly estimated knowing the radiation output and the patient’s size.

Different kinds of radiation have different effects on the human tissue, even if the absorbed dose is the same. In radiology, the only type of radiation used is X-rays. However, in nuclear medicine, radiotherapy and industrial exposure, other types of radiation such as electrons, protons and α-particles are commonly used. To be able to compare the effects of these types of radiation on the human body, the equiva­ lent dose is used. The equivalent dose is the product of the absorbed dose and a radiation weighting factor (W ), which is spe-

R cifific for the type of radiation that is used (Equivalent dose = absorbed dose x W ).

R The equivalent dose is measured in sievert (1 Sv = 1 J/kg).

In practice, it is a sporadic occurrence that the entire body is homogeneously exposed to radiation. Moreover, as discussed in the previous chapter, different tissues have different susceptibilities to radiation damage. Therefore, if one wishes to make a more precise estimation of the biological risks associated with radiation, these factors must also be considered by using the effective dose. Each tissue type (lung, thyroid, liver, skin etc.) has a specifific tissue weighting factor(W ), proportional

T to the risk of developing cancer in that specifific tissue. As a result, the effective dose is calculated as the sum of the equivalent doses taken by each tissue, each multiplied by their respective tissue weighting factors (Effective dose = Σ absorbed dose x W

10.2.3. Exposure of the medical personnel Deterministic effects

There is no risk of deterministic effects for diagnostic radiologists.

Interventional radiologists are exposed to higher doses of radiation with potential deterministic effects on the skin and the lens. Dermatitis of the hands was frequently reported in the early days of radiology, but nowadays, it is entirely avoidable if adequate safety measures are followed.

Cataract is the only deterministic effect with signifificant clinical implications for interventional radiologists as their life-long doses are often exceeding the deterministic threshold. Recent studies have shown that the lens is much more sensitive to radiation than previously believed, showing high interindividual variability. There is evidence that the pathogenetic mechanism for cataract could be, in fact, stochastic. There is no risk for sterility among both diagnostic and interventional radiologists, as the life-long doses they receive are well below the deterministic threshold for women and men.

Stochastic effects

Current knowledge shows that diagnostic radiologists have the same risk of dying from cancer as other categories of physicians. In contrast, interventional radiologists might have a theoretically slightly increased risk, but there is no defifinitive data to prove it.

There is a negligible risk for deterministic and stochastic effects on the fetus regarding pregnant or potentially pregnant interventional radiologists. Therefore, if appropriate radiation protection measures are taken, pregnant female interventional radiologists (and, of course, diagnostic radiologists) can carry on with their work if they choose to do so with no signifificant risk to their baby.

10.3. Radioprotection

Since the early days of radiology, after the fifirst adverse effects of radiation had been noticed on both patients and medical practitioners, safety measures started being established to limit these effects. On an international level, the International Com- mission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) issues non-binding guidelines, which are often adopted by the corresponding national organizations. Radioprotection regulations vary between different countries, but some common concepts will be discussed further.

10.3.1. Radioprotection of the patient

Patient radioprotection revolves around two main concepts: justifification and optimization.

The justifification concept is based on the need for a radiological examination or procedure to do more good than harm. This has to be taken into account on national or institutional levels, such as deciding whether the use of mammography for breast cancer screening is appropriate and on individual levels, such as deciding whether to perform a CT on a pregnant woman that has suffered a car accident.

A radiological examination request needs to be adequately justifified by the referring clinician based on the patients’ clinical and biological fifindings. The clinician must formulate one or more specifific questions that they expect the examination to help answering. The possibility of other, less irradiating alternatives must always be excluded before requesting the examination. The request needs to be reviewed and accepted by the radiologist, who can reject it if considered inappropriate. The exposure to radiation needs the patient’s consent, who has the right to reject the procedure. Whereas regulations in this regard vary between countries, it is advisable to always ask for written consent from pregnant or potentially pregnant women as well as from the parents of pediatric patients.

Protection optimization relies on the concept that the patient should receive

a dose as low as reasonably achievable

(ALARA) for an examination enabling a correct diagnosis while considering social and economic factors.

This is achieved by a series of measures such as using only authorized medical equip- ment with a regular maintenance schedule and having adequately trained personnel. Protective lead aprons reduce exposure to nontarget sensitive organs such as the gonads and the breasts in young women. Women at reproductive age should always be asked whether they might be pregnant and perform the examination during the fifirst ten days after the last menstrual period.

There are no mandatory patient dose limits for diagnostic imaging. However, diagnostic reference levels have been established to help practitioners know whether the patient dose received from a specifific examination is unusually low or high and take corrective actions. Reference I0. DOSIMETRY AND RADIOPROTECTION l 91 levels are benefificial in screening programs, pediatric radiology, and highly irradiating procedures such as CT and flfluoroscopy.

Some of the basic technical procedures which can be undertaken to reduce patient iradiation are:

  • Use higher kV whenever possible;
  • Filter the primary beam;
  • Strictly limit the exposed fifield/volume;
  • Use appropriate focus - patient distance;
  • Use shields (aprons, organ protectors) for sensitive and non-target organs;
  • Use the Bucky grid;
  • Use high sensitivity detectors;
  • Reduce mAs as much as possible;
  • Reduce exposure time;
  • Reduce exposure number.

10.3.2. Radioprotection of the medical personnel

Radiation exposure to medical staff is a form of occupational exposure that should also follow the ALARA principle. Dose limits for occupational exposure have been established in order to avoid unacceptable risks caused by radiation exposure.

The radiation exposure of the personnel in a radiology department is monitored using small dosimeters mandatory to be worn at work.

In the case of personnel working in diagnostic radiology only, one dosimeter worn on the front of the torso is suffificient.

In interventional radiology, at least one dosimeter needs to be worn under and another outside the apron.

The dosimeters are usually read once a month and an investigation needs to be undertaken if abnormally high doses are recorded. The personnel’s constant monitoring is needed to assure their safety and serve as an indicator of correct radioprotection procedures in the department.

Staff working exclusively in diagnostic radiology do not need to be close to the pa92 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS tient during radiation exposure. Therefore, they are protected both by distance (“inverse square law”) and by a physical shielding barrier incorporated in the scanning chamber wall and window. Therefore, for this staff category, occupational doses are very low, and most of them do not receive any measurable doses at all.

However, staff working in an interventional radiology department are exposed to higher radiation levels, in rare situations approaching and even exceeding the dose limits. This category of personnel needs to work in the patients’ proximity while exposed to radiation; therefore, additional safety measures are mandatory. The interventionalist needs to wear lead aprons protecting the neck, trunk and upper limbs, and protective eyewear and use mobile lead shields whenever possible. They need to stay as far as possible from the radiation fifield and limit exposure duration.
